newsitem.title: TURKEY: Emerging gold producers gaining ground on big four.
newsitem.headline: Emerging gold producers gaining ground on big four.

text.p: Gold output in Latin America, Asia and parts of the former Soviet Union is seen growing more rapidly than in South Africa, the U.S., Australia and Canada, the chief executive of Gold Fields Mineral Services said on Wednesday.

"Although the outlook for both North America and Australia remains positive and the worst is probably over in South Africa, the developing regions of the world such as Latin America, Asia and parts of the CIS (Commonwealth on Independent States) are likely to outstrip any growth in production in the big four," said Stewart Murray of the London-based company.

He told the International Gold Markets conference in Istanbul that the big four's share of total world output fell to 55 percent last year, the lowest for more than a century and compared with 80 percent in earlier years.
"It would seem likely that, in the next five years, the big four will lose their special status held for nearly 150 years of producing more than half the world's annual production," he said.
But he said most of the new mine development projects were being undertaken by companies based in the big four, although their home countries would no longer be the focus for new mines.
"We can be assured that the companies from the big four countries will maintain their dominance of world mine production," he said.
World mine production rose to 1,120 tonnes in the first half of this year, up by 34 tonnes over the same 1995 period, with the big four responsible for 13 tonnes of this increase.

Murray said output from South Africa, the world's largest producer of gold, would have fallen by 20 percent, or over 120 tonnes, by the end of this year from the level in 1993 on the assumption that the trend in the first half of this year would continue in the second half.

A decline in productivity in the labour-intensive South African mining industry, a drop in the amount of gold-bearing ores under treatment and a possible increase in gold theft were the main reasons leading to the decline in South African output.

Large-scale projects in North America would help raise gold production by about 10 percent in the next two years, including output from Meikle mine, Pipeline mine in Nevada and Alaska's Fort Knox operation where about 30 tonnes are expected, he said.
Murray said Canadian production was showing good growth again with help from new projects.

"Although the annual output from these new operations is not in the same league as those in the United States, they should, nonetheless, provide a significant boost to the country's production over the next five years," he said.

Expressing his optimism about developments in Australia, Murray said exploration expenditure has picked up considerably over the past few years and "although there have been several major discoveries, there must still be plenty to be found."
He said companies were directing their efforts towards current mines and this was increasing reserves in many existing mines.
